analysis.one_liner: Requires warrants before the government searches Americans' communications collected under foreign surveillance law.
analysis.headline: The Government Surveillance Reform Act, introduced November 7, 2023 with 10 bipartisan cosponsors, was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee and never received a hearing or vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would put a judge's warrant requirement around the government's searches of Americans' communications collected under Section 702 of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act, a program that sweeps in ordinary people's emails and texts because they communicate with foreigners overseas. It would also block the FBI from buying Americans' personal data from data brokers, require warrants for location and web-browsing records, end "abouts" collection, impose discipline for employees who violate surveillance rules, and let Americans sue over unlawful spying. In exchange, it would extend the underlying Section 702 program for four more years, through September 2027.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary Americans whose calls, emails, and location data can currently be searched by federal agents without a warrant, simply because those communications were swept up while targeting foreigners abroad. It also benefits tech and telecom providers, who gain a court process before they can be forced to help the government spy, and it protects everyone whose data is currently sold to law enforcement by data brokers.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Everyday users of phones and email

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits government officials from searching the communications of U.S. persons without a probable-cause warrant, with narrow exceptions for emergencies, consent, and cybersecurity signatures.
Prohibits law enforcement from purchasing Americans' personal data from data brokers and extends warrant protections to location information, web browsing records, search queries, and emails.
Bans the warrantless acquisition of domestic communications and bars 'reverse targeting' — spying on a foreign target for the real purpose of reading an American's messages.
Ends the authority to resume 'abouts' collection, which captures communications that merely mention a target, and imposes five-year retention limits on data collected about Americans.

Limits use of 702-collected information against Americans in criminal, civil, and administrative proceedings to a narrow list of serious threats, and creates escalating discipline — up to termination and loss of security clearance — for federal employees who violate the rules.

Creates accountability in the secret surveillance court by requiring disclosure of exculpatory information in applications, protecting against judge shopping by the Justice Department, expanding amicus advocates, declassifying significant court decisions, and letting Americans sue over unlawful surveillance without being blocked by the state secrets privilege.

analysis.who_pays: Federal intelligence and law enforcement agencies (the FBI, CIA, and NSA) lose the ability to query Americans' communications without a warrant and to buy data brokers' files; data brokers lose a law-enforcement customer base; and telecom and tech providers face some new court processes, though they gain protection from unchecked government demands. The bill's own extension keeps the 702 program operating through September 2027, so the cost to the intelligence community is its unchecked access to Americans' data, not the program's existence.

drawbacks.text: The bill extends Section 702, the sweeping foreign-intelligence collection program, for four more years through September 2027, so it locks in the very program it reforms; critics who wanted the authority to lapse outright would point to that trade.

It leaves significant carve-outs: emergency warrantless searches are allowed, evidence from a denied emergency authorization is suppressed in court but can still be disclosed with Attorney General approval if it signals a threat of death or serious bodily harm, and the Attorney General retains approval power over use of 702 information in proceedings.

The standard national-security objection is that warrant requirements for 702 queries would slow terrorism and counterintelligence cases; the bill's answer is its emergency exception, but agencies argue any friction in bulk databases creates risk, and the FBI and intelligence community publicly fought warrant requirements during the 2023-2024 reauthorization debate.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real and broad: a warrant requirement before the government reads Americans' swept-up messages, plus a stop to law enforcement buying data brokers' files, would change the daily privacy of tens of millions of people. The main cost is to government efficiency in intelligence work, which the bill addresses with emergency and cybersecurity exceptions. The genuine structural weakness is the four-year extension of 702 itself — reformers get warrants, the agencies get certainty — and some would argue the bill legitimizes a program it should have narrowed more sharply. On balance, the protections for ordinary people outweigh the trade.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in the Senate and referred to the Judiciary Committee, which never held a hearing or vote on it before the two-year Congress ended, so it died without any action.

narrative.text: Senator Ron Wyden introduced the bill on November 7, 2023, joined by nine original cosponsors spanning both parties, including Republican Senators Mike Lee, Cynthia Lummis, and Steve Daines.
It received 10 cosponsors total, 7 Democrats and 3 Republicans, and was read twice and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee.
The action history shows no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action at any point afterward; the Congress ended January 3, 2025 with the bill still sitting in committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The intelligence and law-enforcement agencies that opposed warrant requirements kept their existing unchecked access to Americans' communications and their ability to buy data brokers' files, and data brokers kept the law-enforcement market. The 118th Congress ended with no reform at all; a separate 2024 law later extended Section 702 without the warrant requirement this bill would have imposed.

for.name: Sen. Ron Wyden
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Government Surveillance Reform Act and recruited a bipartisan group of original cosponsors.

for.name: Sen. Mike Lee
for.what_they_did: Signed on as an original cosponsor, giving the reform bill bipartisan cover from the right.

for.name: Sens. Baldwin, Lummis, Hirono, Daines, Tester, Warren, and Markey
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, bringing it to 10 cosponsors (7 Democrats, 3 Republicans).

for.name: Privacy and civil liberties organizations
for.what_they_did: Publicly urged passage of surveillance warrant requirements during the 2023-2024 Section 702 reauthorization debate.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral on November 7, 2023 and took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: FBI and intelligence community leadership
against.what_they_did: Publicly lobbied against warrant requirements for 702 queries during the reauthorization fight, warning they would hamper counterterrorism work.

against.name: Senate leadership
against.what_they_did: Never brought surveillance reform to the floor, letting the 702 debate play out on a separate reauthorization bill without these warrant protections.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was genuinely bipartisan — 7 Democrats and 3 Republicans including libertarian-leaning Senator Mike Lee — so the bill's death was procedural, not a party-line vote that never happened.

industries.note: Section 508 would prohibit law enforcement from purchasing Americans' personal data from brokers, and 509 imposes consistent privacy protections on broker-held data. Brokers currently sell location, browsing, and communications-derived data to government agencies in a legal gray area, a practice this bill ends.

industries.industry: Federal intelligence and law enforcement agencies
industries.note: The FBI, CIA, NSA, and related agencies would lose the power to query Americans' communications without a warrant, to collect 'abouts' communications, and to buy broker data, and would face escalating discipline up to termination for violations. The bill still extends their core 702 authority for four years.

industries.industry: Electronic communication service providers (telecom and tech platforms)
industries.note: Section 106 would bar the government from forcing technical assistance without a court finding it is necessary and narrowly tailored, and providers would not be obligated to comply absent an explicit court order — a shield against unchecked demands. In exchange, the bill extends the 702 program under which they receive directives for four more years.
